articles.title: Low-fat diets do not prevent dementia deaths in older women
articles.summary: A large clinical trial tracked nearly 50,000 postmenopausal women for two decades to see if a low-fat diet could prevent dementia deaths. The results suggest that changing your diet later in life might not stop severe cognitive decline.

articles.title: Mood symptoms in bipolar disorder correlate with changes in sexual desire and distress
articles.summary: A six-month study found that depressive symptoms and day-to-day emotional instability are linked to decreased sexual desire and increased sexual distress in people newly diagnosed with bipolar disorder.

articles.title: New study finds narcissism is linked to violent intentions on both sides of the abortion debate
articles.summary: Pro-choice and pro-life Americans sit on opposite sides of one of the country’s most heated debates. But among those willing to use illegal or violent tactics, a new study finds a common thread: a hostile, manipulative form of narcissism.

articles.title: Intelligence alone may not win you status. A new evolutionary psychology study hints at what does.
articles.summary: People may reward intelligence for what it can do for the group rather than for its own sake. A new study found that the link between students’ test scores and the respect they earned appeared to run through how well they solved a group coordination problem.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? articles.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
articles.summary: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.

articles.title: Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
articles.summary: Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

articles.title: A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
articles.summary: Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.

articles.title: People who favor science over religious dogma are surprisingly open to believing in ghosts and magic
articles.summary: As traditional religious affiliations decline, supernatural beliefs are not vanishing. A new survey reveals that people who favor secular reasoning over religious authority often hold magical or superstitious beliefs, provided they maintain some residual connection to spirituality.

articles.title: Expecting entitlement, researchers asked young men about sex. What they found was fear, vigilance, and shame.
articles.summary: Some young men may have absorbed a cultural suspicion of men so deeply that they see themselves as potential perpetrators, according to an interview study that found fear and shame crowding out pleasure in their accounts of sex.

articles.title: Six future Trump officials wrote books before taking office. All six leaned hardest on the same metaphor.
articles.summary: Before joining the second Trump administration, J. D. Vance, Marco Rubio, Pete Hegseth, and three other future officials wrote books that framed politics largely through metaphors of war, decline, disease, and betrayal. Metaphors of threat outnumbered metaphors of renewal by about nine to one.

articles.summary: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on.
